cells.document: Second London Baptist Confession of Faith
cells.date: first published 1677; endorsed by the General Assembly in London, 3-12 September 1689
cells.excerpt: not from anything at all foreseen in man, nor from any power or agency in the creature, being wholly passive therein, being dead in sins and trespasses
cells.shows: The confession teaches that the effectual call is of God's grace alone and that the person is wholly passive in it until renewed by the Holy Spirit.

cells.document: Second London Baptist Confession of Faith
cells.section: Chapter 30, Of the Lord's Supper, paragraph 7
cells.excerpt: do then also inwardly by faith, really and indeed, yet not carnally and corporally, but spiritually receive, and feed upon Christ crucified, and all the benefits of his death
cells.shows: The confession teaches that worthy receivers spiritually feed on Christ in the Supper by faith, while denying a bodily presence; paragraph 2 of the same chapter also calls the Supper 'only a memorial' of Christ's one offering, against the sacrifice of the mass.

cells.document: Second London Baptist Confession of Faith
cells.excerpt: Those who do actually profess repentance towards God, faith in, and obedience to, our Lord Jesus Christ, are the only proper subjects of this ordinance.
cells.shows: The confession restricts baptism to those who profess faith, and calls it an ordinance and a sign; this is the believer's-baptism half of the middle position, paired with the spiritual-feeding language of chapter 30.

cells.document: Second London Baptist Confession of Faith
cells.section: Chapter 1, Of the Holy Scriptures, paragraph 1 (final clause)
cells.excerpt: which maketh the Holy Scriptures to be most necessary, those former ways of God's revealing his will unto his people being now ceased.
cells.shows: The confession says that God's former ways of revealing his will have ceased now that revelation is committed to writing; it speaks of revelation and does not name tongues, prophecy or healing.

cells.document: Second London Baptist Confession of Faith
cells.excerpt: consists of the whole number of the elect, that have been, are, or shall be gathered into one, under Christ, the head thereof
cells.shows: The confession defines the universal church as the whole number of the elect of every age gathered into one under Christ, which is a single people of God.

cells.document: Second London Baptist Confession of Faith
cells.excerpt: it is alone by the grace of this covenant that all the posterity of fallen Adam that ever were saved did obtain life and blessed immortality
cells.shows: The confession teaches one covenant of grace, revealed by steps from Adam to the New Testament, by which everyone ever saved was saved.

cells.document: Second London Baptist Confession of Faith
cells.section: Chapter 1, Of the Holy Scriptures, paragraph 6 (see also paragraphs 1 and 10)
cells.excerpt: unto which nothing at any time is to be added, whether by new revelation of the Spirit, or traditions of men.
cells.shows: The confession holds that Scripture contains the whole counsel of God and that neither new revelation nor tradition may add to it; paragraph 10 makes Scripture the supreme judge over councils and ancient writers.

cells.document: Second London Baptist Confession of Faith
cells.section: Chapter 22, Of Religious Worship and the Sabbath Day, paragraph 1
cells.excerpt: instituted by himself, and so limited by his own revealed will, that he may not be worshipped according to the imagination and devices of men
cells.shows: The confession limits acceptable worship to what God has prescribed in Scripture (the regulative principle); it does not mention set liturgies or the church calendar by name.

cells.document: Second London Baptist Confession of Faith
cells.excerpt: The reading of the Scriptures, preaching, and hearing the Word of God, teaching and admonishing one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs
cells.shows: The confession lists the parts of worship as Scripture reading, preaching, song, baptism and the Lord's Supper, which matches the free pole's own description of a service ordered around Word, prayer, song and ordinances.

notes: All six axes are cited to one document, the Second London Baptist Confession, which is the defining and subscribed standard of this tradition (public domain, so no link-only cells). Dates were checked on the Wikipedia article for the confession (first published London 1677; endorsed by representatives of over 100 churches, 3-12 September 1689). TEXT EDITIONS: the1689confession.com carries a lightly modernised text (e.g. 'shows' for 'shews'); in chapter 1.1 it prints 'being now completed', whereas the original reads 'being now ceased'. For the gifts cell the original wording was therefore taken from the Wikisource transcription, which was opened and reads 'being now ceased'. If the site quotes 1.1 it should use the original wording and link to Wikisource. Every excerpt was copied from the page opened, not from memory. CAVEATS: (1) Gifts 95: the confession speaks only of the ceasing of revelation; cessationist Reformed Baptists read 1.1 and 1.6 ('new revelation of the Spirit') as excluding continuing prophecy and tongues, but the text does not name the gifts, so the citation is weaker than the coordinate. No separate binding Reformed Baptist statement on the gifts was opened; none found beyond the confession. (2) Kingdom 5: the confession predates dispensationalism and does not address a rapture or a future national kingdom for Israel; it supports the one-people pole through 26.1 and 7.3 and is silent on the millennium. Note that 1689 federalism differs from Presbyterian covenant theology on how the old covenants relate to the covenant of grace, but both hold one people of God. (3) Worship 88: the confession gives the regulative principle and the list of elements, from which holders infer no prescribed liturgy or calendar; it does not say so in terms, and many Reformed Baptist churches keep a plain, settled order. (4) Table 50: chapter 30.7 (spiritual feeding) and 30.2 ('only a memorial', said against the mass) together with 29.2 (professing believers only) fit the audited middle position and the axis's own 'between' sentence. The confession uses 'ordinance' throughout, not 'sacrament'.
